questions.prompt: Put the lifecycle of a refresh token in order.
steps: Issuance: the user logs in and gets a short-lived access token and a long-lived refresh token
Access and depletion: the client uses the access token for API requests until it expires
Refreshing: the client sends the refresh token to get a brand new access token
Rotation: the server issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one
questions.explanation: The refresh token is created once at login; after that, each refresh swaps an expired access token for a new one and, with rotation, replaces the refresh token too.

questions.prompt: In the hand-rolled design, what does the `RefreshTokens` table store for each refresh token?
options: The raw token string, so it can be compared directly
The token encrypted with the RSA private key
Only a SHA-256 hash of the token, like a password
Nothing; refresh tokens are validated from their signature alone
questions.explanation: The raw value only ever exists in the HTTP response and the client's storage. On refresh the server recomputes the hash and looks up the row by `TokenHash`.

source.section: Why refresh tokens exist in the first place

questions.prompt: A valid refresh token rt-001 is used at `/api/auth/refresh`. What does the server do with it?
options: Keeps rt-001 valid until it expires and issues a new access token only
Revokes rt-001 now, issues rt-002 in the same token family and sets rt-001's `ReplacedByTokenId` to rt-002
Revokes rt-001 and starts a new token family for rt-002
Deletes every refresh token the user has and asks for the password again
questions.explanation: That is rotation: the old token dies immediately even though it hadn't expired, and the replacement joins the same family so the chain can be traced.

source.section: Why refresh tokens exist in the first place

questions.prompt: The real user is on rt-004 when an attacker presents the stolen, already-revoked rt-002. What happens?
options: Only rt-002 is rejected; the real user's rt-004 keeps working
The attacker receives rt-005, because rt-002 belongs to a valid family
The server revokes the whole family, rt-004 included, so the real user must log in again
The server ignores the request because rt-002 has not expired
questions.explanation: A legitimate client never presents an already-revoked token, so this is treated as theft. The server can't tell who is real, so it burns the whole family and forces a fresh login.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say rotation and reuse detection are needed together?
options: Without reuse detection a stolen token starts its own silent chain; without rotation nothing changes between calls, so theft can't be detected
Rotation makes tokens shorter, and reuse detection makes them expire sooner
Rotation is needed for access tokens and reuse detection for refresh tokens
Either one alone is enough; using both only improves performance
questions.explanation: Rotation alone lets an attacker's chain run in parallel with the user's forever. Reuse detection alone has no "this token was already used" moment to catch.

source.section: Why refresh tokens exist in the first place

questions.prompt: How is an OpenIddict refresh token (default mode) different from the hand-built access token JWT?
options: It is a bare random string with no claims, just like the hand-rolled refresh token
It is signed but not encrypted, so anyone can read its claims
It carries claims but is encrypted with ASP.NET Core Data Protection, so it is opaque without the server's keys
It is hashed with SHA-256, so not even the server can read it
questions.explanation: A JWT is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can decode its payload. The OpenIddict refresh token is self-contained but encrypted, so a leaked copy only reveals ciphertext.
